text.ch-anatomy:
CHAPTER 1 OF 4 · EYE BLOCKS

Anatomy: the orbit and its nerves

Each orbit is an irregular pyramid: its base at the front, its apex pointing back and medially to the optic foramen. It is 40–50 mm deep and holds about 30 ml, of which the globe and the muscle cone take about 7 ml; the rest is loose connective tissue and fat. The four recti run from the apex to the globe and form the muscle cone. Inside the cone (intraconal) run the optic nerve, the ophthalmic artery and the nerves to the muscles; outside it (extraconal) is more fat.

FUNCTION	NERVES	REMEMBER
Movement (akinesia)
III: superior, inferior and medial recti, inferior oblique. IV: superior oblique. VI: lateral rectus.
LR6 SO4; III, IV and VI all need blocking for a still eye
Sensation
V1: nasociliary, lacrimal and frontal branches, through the superior orbital fissure
Pain from the cornea: Aδ and C fibres in V1
Vision
II (optic nerve)
Often temporarily lost after a needle block
Lid closure
VII (orbicularis oculi)
Peribulbar blocks usually reach it; retrobulbar may not
Autonomic
Parasympathetic from the Edinger–Westphal nucleus with III, via the ciliary ganglion; sympathetic from T1 via the superior cervical ganglion

The ophthalmic artery (from the internal carotid) enters through the optic canal; in elderly and hypertensive patients it is tortuous and easy to injure.

KEY POINT

Axial length

The distance from the cornea to the retina, about 25 mm in adults (12–35 mm), measured before cataract surgery. Long (myopic) eyes are more easily perforated.

text.ch-peri:
CHAPTER 2 OF 4 · EYE · NEEDLE BLOCKS

Peribulbar and retrobulbar blocks

Needle blocks that give anaesthesia and akinesia of the eye. A peribulbar block puts a larger volume outside the muscle cone; a retrobulbar block puts a smaller volume inside it, close to the optic nerve. The retrobulbar block is now rarely used because of its risks. In Singapore these blocks are usually done by ophthalmologists; the anaesthetist must know the technique and manage the complications.

USE IT FOR

Intraocular surgery needing a still eye: vitreoretinal surgery, complex cataract, trabeculectomy
When topical anaesthesia is not suitable
POSITION
Supine, looking straight ahead
PROBE
None: landmarks
NEEDLE
25G; about 25 mm (peribulbar), longer for retrobulbar
DOSE
Peribulbar 8–10 ml; retrobulbar 4–5 ml
COVERS
Globe anaesthesia and akinesia (peribulbar also the lids)

Schematic section drawn by this page, not to scale. Use the arrow keys on the image to step through.

Position

Supine, head on a pillow, looking straight ahead (looking up and in brings the optic nerve closer to the needle). Full monitoring and an intravenous cannula.

Equipment
25G needle: about 16–25 mm for peribulbar; needles longer than 25 mm carry more risk to the optic nerve, but shorter needles do not remove it.
Local anaesthetic with hyaluronidase; a soft pad or Honan balloon
Landmarks and technique

Peribulbar. Through the lower lid (or conjunctiva), inferotemporally, lateral to the lateral limbus. Straight back, parallel to the orbital floor, to about 25 mm; if you touch bone, angle slightly up. The tip lies outside the cone, beyond the equator of the globe but in front of its back surface. Aspirate, inject 8–10 ml. Brisk conjunctival swelling means the tip is too superficial. Press gently, then test after 5 minutes.

Supplementary injections (up to 5 ml) if movement remains: medial canthus (through the conjunctiva medial to the caruncle, parallel to the medial wall) or superonasal (through the upper lid above the medial limbus, aiming away from the globe).

Retrobulbar. Same entry point, bevel facing the globe; straight back until the equator is passed (10–15 mm), then up and medially into the cone, to the level of the back of the globe. Keep the tip from crossing medial to the axis of the globe: the optic nerve is in the medial half. Aspirate, inject 4–5 ml, then press. A separate lid block may be needed.

Sonoanatomy

The orbit is a pyramid about 40–50 mm deep, about 30 ml in volume, its axis pointing back and medially to the apex. The globe and muscle cone take up about 7 ml; the rest is fat. The axial length of the globe is about 25 mm (12–35 mm). Long eyes (myopia, axial length over 25 mm) are easier to perforate.

SUPERFICIAL TO DEEP

Orbital fat
Target and deposition

Peribulbar: the extraconal fat beyond the equator. Retrobulbar: the intraconal fat at the back of the globe. Both work by local anaesthetic reaching the nerves to the extraocular muscles (III, IV, VI) and the sensory nerves (V1) in and around the cone.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

8–10 ml peribulbar; 4–5 ml retrobulbar

Supplementary injections up to 5 ml.

Local anaesthetic toxicity: Even a small volume injected into an artery or under the optic nerve sheath reaches the brain: monitor ECG, blood pressure and oxygen saturation, keep talking to the patient, and have resuscitation equipment ready.

Coverage

Covers: Anaesthesia and akinesia of the globe. A peribulbar block usually also stops the eyelids closing (orbicularis oculi).

MECHANISM

Akinesia needs III (superior, inferior and medial recti, inferior oblique), IV (superior oblique) and VI (lateral rectus): LR6 SO4, the rest III. Sensation is mainly from V1 (nasociliary, lacrimal and frontal branches).

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Retrobulbar: faster and more reliable, with a smaller volume, lower orbital pressure and less chemosis. Peribulbar: slower (at least 5 minutes) and a bigger volume, so more chemosis and a bigger rise in intraocular pressure, but fewer serious complications and better lid akinesia.

WHAT IT MISSES
The lids, after a retrobulbar block (a separate facial nerve or lid block may be needed).
Superior oblique movement is often the last to go: a supplementary injection may be needed.
Complications and how to avoid them
Brainstem anaesthesia: local anaesthetic under the optic nerve sheath reaches the brainstem. Confusion, apnoea, cardiovascular collapse, sometimes after a delay: ventilate and support.
Intravascular injection: seizures and cardiovascular collapse.
Retrobulbar haemorrhage (1–2%): sudden proptosis, a tense eye and lid. Tell the surgeon at once; the pressure may need urgent relief. Watch the ECG: the oculocardiac reflex can fire.
Globe perforation (under 1%): more likely with long myopic eyes. Pain and loss of vision, or no symptoms; a soft eye. Injecting into the globe can be catastrophic.
Optic nerve injury (under 1%), extraocular muscle injury (later squint), chemosis, corneal abrasion.
Practical pearls
Looking straight ahead keeps the optic nerve away from the needle; looking up and in brings it closer.
Stay lateral (inferotemporal) and do not cross the axis of the globe.
Check the axial length before the block: over 25 mm, think about a sub-Tenon’s or topical technique.
Drugs for eye blocks

Lidocaine 2% (5–10 ml gives about 90 minutes), often mixed with bupivacaine 0.75% for a longer block; no stronger than 2% lidocaine because of muscle toxicity. Hyaluronidase (commonly 1–7.5 units/ml) helps the local anaesthetic spread, lowers orbital pressure and improves the block. Adrenaline is usually avoided.

Exam corner

PRACTICE QUESTION (VIVA)

Compare peribulbar and retrobulbar blocks. What are the serious complications and how would you manage brainstem anaesthesia?

Model answer points
Peribulbar: extraconal, 8–10 ml, slower onset, more chemosis and pressure, fewer serious complications, better lid akinesia.
Retrobulbar: intraconal, 4–5 ml, faster and denser, closer to the optic nerve: optic nerve injury, retrobulbar haemorrhage, brainstem anaesthesia.
Others: globe perforation (long myopic eyes), intravascular injection, muscle injury.
Brainstem anaesthesia: call for help, airway and ventilation (it may cause apnoea), circulatory support; it wears off as the local anaesthetic is redistributed.

text.ch-st:
CHAPTER 3 OF 4 · EYE · CANNULA BLOCK

Sub-Tenon’s block

Local anaesthetic through a blunt cannula into the potential space between Tenon’s capsule and the sclera. It spreads round the back of the globe into the cone. No sharp needle goes into the back of the orbit, so the risk of perforation, optic nerve injury and brainstem anaesthesia is even lower.

USE IT FOR

Cataract and most intraocular surgery
Patients on anticoagulants (major bleeding is rare)
Long myopic eyes, where a needle block is riskier
POSITION
Supine, looking up and out
PROBE
None: direct vision
NEEDLE
Blunt curved 19G sub-Tenon’s cannula, 25 mm
DOSE
4–5 ml (2–3 ml more if needed)
COVERS
Globe anaesthesia; akinesia varies with the volume

Schematic section drawn by this page, not to scale. Use the arrow keys on the image to step through.

Position

Supine. The operator stands at the head; the patient looks up and out to expose the inferonasal quadrant.

Equipment
Topical local anaesthetic drops; povidone-iodine 5%
Small lid speculum, non-toothed forceps, blunt spring scissors
Blunt curved 19G sub-Tenon’s cannula (25 mm)
Technique
Topical anaesthetic into the lower fornix (a drop of adrenaline 1:10 000 reduces bleeding), then povidone-iodine 5%.
Speculum in. Patient looks up and out.
In the inferonasal quadrant, lift the conjunctiva and Tenon’s capsule together and make an opening no more than 2 mm wide down to the sclera, 5–10 mm from the limbus.
Pass the cannula through the opening and follow the curve of the globe, staying on the sclera, to 15–20 mm, behind the equator.
Aspirate and inject 4–5 ml slowly; 2–3 ml more if akinesia is not enough. Gentle pressure on the closed eye.
Sonoanatomy

SUPERFICIAL TO DEEP

Orbital fat
Target and deposition

The sub-Tenon’s space behind the equator. If the fluid leaks back out of the opening, the cannula is not far enough back.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

4–5 ml of local anaesthetic (2–3 ml more if needed)

Local anaesthetic toxicity: Even a small volume injected into an artery or under the optic nerve sheath reaches the brain: monitor ECG, blood pressure and oxygen saturation, keep talking to the patient, and have resuscitation equipment ready.

Coverage

Covers: Anaesthesia of the globe; akinesia depends on the volume.

MECHANISM

The local anaesthetic spreads round the back of the globe in the sub-Tenon’s space and diffuses into the retrobulbar space, reaching the sensory and motor nerves.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Reliable anaesthesia. Akinesia is variable and volume-dependent; onset is slower than a retrobulbar block (at least 5 minutes).

WHAT IT MISSES
Full akinesia with small volumes.
Complications and how to avoid them
Chemosis and subconjunctival haemorrhage (common): can get in the surgeon’s way.
Leak from the opening: a weaker block.
Rare but reported: orbital and retrobulbar haemorrhage, globe perforation, central spread, orbital cellulitis.
Avoid after previous surgery that scars the space (scleral buckle, retinal or glaucoma surgery).

text.ch-topical:
CHAPTER 4 OF 4 · EYE BLOCKS

Topical anaesthesia and choosing a technique

Drops or gel on the cornea and conjunctiva: the simplest technique, and enough on its own for short, uncomplicated surgery such as phacoemulsification through a small corneal incision.

TECHNIQUE

Drops or gel: for example tetracaine 0.75%, proxymetacaine (proparacaine) 0.5% or lidocaine 2% gel. Gel gives more drug in the anterior chamber, but put it on after the antiseptic.
Put drops into the conjunctival sac, not straight onto the cornea: they can cloud it.
The surgeon may add intracameral preservative-free lidocaine 1% into the anterior chamber, for the discomfort of hydrodissection.
Which technique
	TOPICAL	SUB-TENON’S	PERIBULBAR	RETROBULBAR
Akinesia
None
Variable, volume-dependent
Good
Good, fast
Onset
Immediate
At least 5 min
At least 5 min
Fast
Volume
Drops
4–5 ml
8–10 ml
4–5 ml
Serious complications
None
Rare
Uncommon
Highest
Best for
Short cataract surgery; anticoagulated; only one seeing eye
Most intraocular surgery; anticoagulated
Surgery needing a still eye
Now rarely used
Downsides
Eye moves; needs a cooperative patient; short; may need sedation
Chemosis, subconjunctival haemorrhage, leak
Chemosis, raised pressure
Optic nerve injury, haemorrhage, brainstem anaesthesia

No large trials compare the techniques for safety or effectiveness; the choice is often personal preference.

When not to do a block
ABSOLUTE	RELATIVE
Patient refusal
Local anaesthetic allergy
Infection or marked inflammation of the orbit
Long myopic eye
Can’t lie flat or still (heart or lung disease, tremor, confusion)
Children; communication difficulties
Bleeding problems or anticoagulation (many still block if the INR is in range; prefer sub-Tenon’s or topical)
Previous scleral buckle; thyroid eye disease or other orbital masses

WARNING

Intraocular pressure

Any injection into the orbit raises the pressure on the globe. Watch for proptosis and feel the eye. Gentle compression (for example a Honan balloon at 20–30 mmHg, never over 30) brings it down; some anaesthetists wait up to 30 minutes before surgery.

STEP 2 OF 4 · IDENTIFY

STEP 3 OF 4 · NEEDLE

Lift the conjunctiva and Tenon’s capsule together with forceps, 5–10 mm from the limbus, and make a cut no more than 2 mm wide with blunt scissors, down to bare sclera. STEP 4 OF 4 · INJECT

Aspirate, then inject 4–5 ml slowly; 2–3 ml more if akinesia is not enough. The fluid spreads round the back of the globe and into the cone. Press gently on the closed eye for a few minutes.

Drugs for eye blocks

Lidocaine 2% (5–10 ml gives about 90 minutes), often mixed with bupivacaine 0.75% for a longer block; no stronger than 2% lidocaine because of muscle toxicity. Hyaluronidase (commonly 1–7.5 units/ml) helps the local anaesthetic spread, lowers orbital pressure and improves the block. Adrenaline is usually avoided.

Exam corner

PRACTICE QUESTION (VIVA)

Compare peribulbar and retrobulbar blocks. What are the serious complications and how would you manage brainstem anaesthesia?

Model answer points
Peribulbar: extraconal, 8–10 ml, slower onset, more chemosis and pressure, fewer serious complications, better lid akinesia.
Retrobulbar: intraconal, 4–5 ml, faster and denser, closer to the optic nerve: optic nerve injury, retrobulbar haemorrhage, brainstem anaesthesia.
Others: globe perforation (long myopic eyes), intravascular injection, muscle injury.
Brainstem anaesthesia: call for help, airway and ventilation (it may cause apnoea), circulatory support; it wears off as the local anaesthetic is redistributed.

CHAPTER 3 OF 4 · EYE · CANNULA BLOCK

Sub-Tenon’s block

Local anaesthetic through a blunt cannula into the potential space between Tenon’s capsule and the sclera. It spreads round the back of the globe into the cone. No sharp needle goes into the back of the orbit, so the risk of perforation, optic nerve injury and brainstem anaesthesia is even lower.

USE IT FOR

Cataract and most intraocular surgery
Patients on anticoagulants (major bleeding is rare)
Long myopic eyes, where a needle block is riskier
POSITION
Supine, looking up and out
PROBE
None: direct vision
NEEDLE
Blunt curved 19G sub-Tenon’s cannula, 25 mm
DOSE
4–5 ml (2–3 ml more if needed)
COVERS
Globe anaesthesia; akinesia varies with the volume

Schematic section drawn by this page, not to scale. Use the arrow keys on the image to step through.

Position

Supine. The operator stands at the head; the patient looks up and out to expose the inferonasal quadrant.

Equipment
Topical local anaesthetic drops; povidone-iodine 5%
Small lid speculum, non-toothed forceps, blunt spring scissors
Blunt curved 19G sub-Tenon’s cannula (25 mm)
Technique
Topical anaesthetic into the lower fornix (a drop of adrenaline 1:10 000 reduces bleeding), then povidone-iodine 5%.
Speculum in. Patient looks up and out.
In the inferonasal quadrant, lift the conjunctiva and Tenon’s capsule together and make an opening no more than 2 mm wide down to the sclera, 5–10 mm from the limbus.
Pass the cannula through the opening and follow the curve of the globe, staying on the sclera, to 15–20 mm, behind the equator.
Aspirate and inject 4–5 ml slowly; 2–3 ml more if akinesia is not enough. Gentle pressure on the closed eye.
Sonoanatomy

SUPERFICIAL TO DEEP

Orbital fat
Target and deposition

The sub-Tenon’s space behind the equator. If the fluid leaks back out of the opening, the cannula is not far enough back.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

4–5 ml of local anaesthetic (2–3 ml more if needed)

Local anaesthetic toxicity: Even a small volume injected into an artery or under the optic nerve sheath reaches the brain: monitor ECG, blood pressure and oxygen saturation, keep talking to the patient, and have resuscitation equipment ready.

Coverage

Covers: Anaesthesia of the globe; akinesia depends on the volume.

MECHANISM

The local anaesthetic spreads round the back of the globe in the sub-Tenon’s space and diffuses into the retrobulbar space, reaching the sensory and motor nerves.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Reliable anaesthesia. Akinesia is variable and volume-dependent; onset is slower than a retrobulbar block (at least 5 minutes).

WHAT IT MISSES
Full akinesia with small volumes.
Complications and how to avoid them
Chemosis and subconjunctival haemorrhage (common): can get in the surgeon’s way.
Leak from the opening: a weaker block.
Rare but reported: orbital and retrobulbar haemorrhage, globe perforation, central spread, orbital cellulitis.
Avoid after previous surgery that scars the space (scleral buckle, retinal or glaucoma surgery).

text.ch-topical:
CHAPTER 4 OF 4 · EYE BLOCKS

Topical anaesthesia and choosing a technique

Drops or gel on the cornea and conjunctiva: the simplest technique, and enough on its own for short, uncomplicated surgery such as phacoemulsification through a small corneal incision.

TECHNIQUE

Drops or gel: for example tetracaine 0.75%, proxymetacaine (proparacaine) 0.5% or lidocaine 2% gel. Gel gives more drug in the anterior chamber, but put it on after the antiseptic.
Put drops into the conjunctival sac, not straight onto the cornea: they can cloud it.
The surgeon may add intracameral preservative-free lidocaine 1% into the anterior chamber, for the discomfort of hydrodissection.
Which technique
	TOPICAL	SUB-TENON’S	PERIBULBAR	RETROBULBAR
Akinesia	None	Variable, volume-dependent	Good	Good, fast
Onset	Immediate	At least 5 min	At least 5 min	Fast
Volume	Drops	4–5 ml	8–10 ml	4–5 ml
Serious complications	None	Rare	Uncommon	Highest
Best for	Short cataract surgery; anticoagulated; only one seeing eye	Most intraocular surgery; anticoagulated	Surgery needing a still eye	Now rarely used
Downsides	Eye moves; needs a cooperative patient; short; may need sedation	Chemosis, subconjunctival haemorrhage, leak	Chemosis, raised pressure	Optic nerve injury, haemorrhage, brainstem anaesthesia

No large trials compare the techniques for safety or effectiveness; the choice is often personal preference.

When not to do a block
ABSOLUTE	RELATIVE

Patient refusal
Local anaesthetic allergy
Infection or marked inflammation of the orbit
	
Long myopic eye
Can’t lie flat or still (heart or lung disease, tremor, confusion)
Children; communication difficulties
Bleeding problems or anticoagulation (many still block if the INR is in range; prefer sub-Tenon’s or topical)
Previous scleral buckle; thyroid eye disease or other orbital masses

WARNING

Intraocular pressure

Any injection into the orbit raises the pressure on the globe. Watch for proptosis and feel the eye. Gentle compression (for example a Honan balloon at 20–30 mmHg, never over 30) brings it down; some anaesthetists wait up to 30 minutes before surgery.

STEP 1 OF 4 · LANDMARKS

Patient supine, looking straight ahead. Feel the inferior orbital rim. The needle goes in through the lower lid (or the conjunctiva) at the junction of the lateral third and medial two-thirds, lateral to the lateral limbus: the inferotemporal quadrant, away from the optic nerve.

STEP 2 OF 4 · IDENTIFY

Know what lies behind: the globe (about 24 mm long; longer in myopic eyes), the muscle cone (the four recti) with the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery inside it, and fat inside and outside the cone. A peribulbar block stays outside the cone; a retrobulbar block goes inside it.

STEP 3 OF 4 · NEEDLE

A short needle (about 25 mm, 25G), bevel facing the globe, goes straight back parallel to the orbital floor. If it touches bone, angle slightly upwards. Stop about 25 mm deep: past the equator of the globe, but in front of its back surface, outside the muscle cone.

STEP 4 OF 4 · INJECT

Aspirate, then inject 8–10 ml slowly (often with hyaluronidase). Watch the eye: some proptosis is expected. If the conjunctiva balloons at once (chemosis), the tip is too superficial. Then press gently on the closed eye (soft pad or Honan balloon, not over 30 mmHg) and test movements after 5 minutes.

STEP 1 OF 4 · LANDMARKS

Topical drops into the lower fornix, then povidone-iodine 5%. A small speculum holds the lids apart. The patient looks up and out (“look at my chin” with you at the head), which exposes the inferonasal quadrant.

STEP 2 OF 4 · IDENTIFY

Tenon’s capsule is a thin layer around the globe. In front it fuses with the conjunctiva near the limbus; behind, with the dura of the optic nerve. The sub-Tenon’s space is the potential space between the capsule and the sclera.

STEP 3 OF 4 · NEEDLE

Lift the conjunctiva and Tenon’s capsule together with forceps, 5–10 mm from the limbus, and make a cut no more than 2 mm wide with blunt scissors, down to bare sclera. Pass a blunt curved cannula (19G, 25 mm) through the opening and follow the curve of the globe, keeping it on the sclera, until it is behind the equator (15–20 mm).

STEP 4 OF 4 · INJECT

Aspirate, then inject 4–5 ml slowly; 2–3 ml more if akinesia is not enough. The fluid spreads round the back of the globe and into the cone. Press gently on the closed eye for a few minutes.
